Creek chub (Semotilus atromaculatus) is a common cyprinid found across much of eastern North America, and its life history exhibits notable variation across its range. Among populations from larger river systems, individuals can attain a total body length of 30.3 centimeters [Li = 30.3 centimeters], a size that is relatively large for a minnow and likely reflects access to more stable foraging conditions in those habitats. This asymptotic length is consistent with the upper end of the size spectrum reported for the genus, though local stream-dwelling populations often remain considerably smaller. The species is a broadcast spawner, with females depositing adhesive eggs over gravel substrates in the spring when water temperatures rise. Mature females typically produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], and field studies have found that a 40.2 centimeter (fork length) individual, maintained at a constant water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], exhibits a daily egg production rate of approximately 6.2 eggs per day, a value that reflects the species' relatively high fecundity among nesting, nest-guarding cyprinids.

Sexual maturation in female Creek chub is marked by the attainment of a specific fork length rather than strictly by age, a pattern common in many stream-dwelling cyprinids where growth rate is highly seasonal. Based on field collections from several Midwestern streams, females reach puberty at a fork length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], a size that is typically achieved during their second growing season. This length-based threshold is independent of water temperature in the sense that it is a morphological benchmark, though the time required to reach it is influenced by local thermal regimes; the original estimates of age at puberty being 1.5 years did not specify the temperature conditions under which that growth occurred. Individuals that grow faster in warmer, more productive streams may reach this fork length earlier in the season, but the 12 centimeter value itself appears to be a consistent marker of the onset of gonadal activity across disparate populations. Reaching this size triggers the initiation of vitellogenesis and the onset of reproductive potential in the following spawning season.

The initial offspring mass in Creek chub is remarkably small, reflecting the early developmental stage at which the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion. Newly hatched alevins have a wet weight at birth of 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a mass derived from the average 1.7 millimeter egg diameter and the assumption of a spherical shape. This extremely low birth weight places the young among the smallest of North American cyprinids at hatching, and it necessitates a brief but intensive period of yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding. The larva is highly transparent upon emergence and relies heavily on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days of life. The small size at hatching also makes the prolarvae highly vulnerable to predation and to drift in swift currents, favoring spawning sites in slower, gravelly pools where the newly emerged sac-fry can find refuge. Despite this fragile start, the yolk-sac period is relatively short, and the larva quickly begins exogenous feeding.

Laboratory studies conducted at a constant thermal regime have provided valuable insight into the maximum lifespan of this species under controlled conditions. Individuals maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] and fed ad libitum throughout their lives have been documented to survive for up to 2,920 days [am = up to 2,920 days], a longevity of approximately eight years that is exceptional among small-bodied stream cyprinids. This lifespan far exceeds the typical 3 to 4 years observed in wild populations of Creek chub, where predation, seasonal flooding, and competition for spawning sites impose heavy mortality on adults. The extended survival in captivity is likely attributable to the absence of these ecological pressures as well as the consistent food supply and stable thermal environment. It suggests that the species possesses a considerable physiological potential for longevity that is rarely realized under natural conditions. Notably, senescence in these captive individuals was gradual, with a decline in feeding activity and fin condition becoming apparent only after the seventh year.

Comparative life-history data place Creek chub at an interesting position among its congeners and other nest-building cyprinids. While the maximum recorded total length of 30.3 centimeters [Li = 30.3 centimeters] is not exceptional for the Semotilus genus, it is substantially larger than that of many syntopic minnows such as the blacknose dace, implying a different ecological role as a potential top minnow in smaller headwater streams. The species' reproductive strategy, characterized by a single annual spawning event and an egg diameter of 1.7 millimeters, produces a neonate that weighs 2.6 milligrams [Wwb = 2.6 milligrams] and is reliant on maternal yolk for its initial survival. This moderate egg size is typical for species that practice paternal nest guarding, as the male clears and defends a gravel depression, providing a safer microhabitat that permits a slightly smaller investment per offspring compared to non-guarding broadcast spawners. The combination of a moderate adult size, protected spawning, and a life span that can reach nearly 3,000 days [am = nearly 3,000 days] under favorable conditions reflects an iteroparous life history that buffers against reproductive failure in unpredictable stream environments.
